---

## ARGUMENT

### I. Article 35's Two-Year Period Is a Condition Precedent, but Its Operation Is Not Immune from Equitable Considerations.

Article 35(1) of the Montreal Convention provides that the right to damages "shall be extinguished if an action is not brought within a period of two years." Article 35(2) adds that "[t]he method of calculating that period shall be determined by the law of the court seised of the case." Convention for the Unification of Certain Rules for International Carriage by Air art. 35, May 28, 1999, S. Treaty Doc. No. 106-45. Plaintiff does not dispute that Article 35 is a condition precedent to suit rather than an ordinary limitations defense. The question is whether Article 35(2) leaves room for the forum's equitable principles. It does.

The Eleventh Circuit has long recognized that equitable tolling is available where a litigant shows "extraordinary circumstances that are both beyond his control and unavoidable even with diligence." *Sandvik v. United States*, 177 F.3d 1269, 1271 (11th Cir. 1999); *accord Arce v. Garcia*, 434 F.3d 1254, 1261 (11th Cir. 2006); *Cadet v. Fla. Dep't of Corr.*, 853 F.3d 1216, 1221–22 (11th Cir. 2017). This Court has applied that doctrine where a statute's text did not foreclose it. *See Justice v. United States*, 6 F.3d 1474, 1479 (11th Cir. 1993).

Article 35(2) expressly delegates the "method of calculating" the period to the forum's law. In this Circuit, that law includes equitable tolling. Treating tolling as part of the calculation of the period gives effect to the delegation without disturbing the Convention's two-year limit. It also respects the Convention's text, because Article 35(2) would be superfluous if it left the forum no calculation rules to apply.

Plaintiff acknowledges that *Narayanan* read Article 35 as foreclosing tolling, and that *Lozano* found the presumption of tolling rebutted for the Hague Convention's one-year period. *Lozano* turned on that treaty's particular text, structure, and objectives. Article 35(2) has no counterpart in the Hague Convention, and its express reference to forum law is what distinguishes this case. Plaintiff respectfully submits that *Narayanan* does not bind this Court and gives Article 35(2)'s delegation too little weight.

Plaintiff's circumstances satisfy the *Sandvik* standard. [Insert record facts: the airline's conduct, any misleading communications, and Plaintiff's diligence.] Those circumstances were beyond Plaintiff's control and unavoidable despite diligence. Equitable tolling therefore renders the complaint timely.

### II. Alternatively, the Airline's Bankruptcy Stay Tolled the Period.

Even if equitable tolling were unavailable, the airline's bankruptcy independently preserved Plaintiff's claim. Filing a bankruptcy petition automatically stays "the commencement or continuation" of any action against the debtor that was or could have been commenced before the petition. 11 U.S.C. § 362(a)(1). In this Circuit, acts taken in violation of the stay are void, not merely voidable. *Parker v. Wendy's Int'l, Inc.*, 365 F.3d 1268, 1271 (11th Cir. 2004); *Jove Eng'g, Inc. v. IRS*, 92 F.3d 1539, 1546–47 (11th Cir. 1996). Plaintiff therefore could not have filed a valid action against the debtor during the stay.

Congress also anticipated this problem. Where a nonbankruptcy law fixes a period for commencing an action against the debtor and that period has not expired before the petition, the period "does not expire until the later of" the original end date or thirty days after notice of the stay's termination. 11 U.S.C. § 108(c). The statute applies by its terms to any "applicable nonbankruptcy law" or "agreement," and the Convention, as a ratified treaty, is such law. Applying § 108(c) here does not contradict Article 35, because Article 35(2) directs the court to calculate the period under forum law, and federal bankruptcy law is part of that law.

Plaintiff filed within the extended period. [Insert petition date, stay termination or discharge date, notice date, and complaint filing date.] The complaint was therefore timely, and dismissal should be reversed.
